subject: Latent growth curve model: negative variances

messages.author: b430763ad49e6cd0
messages.subject: Latent growth curve model: negative variances
parts:
Hey,

The model I am trying to fit contains 5 different manifest variables, observed at 4 time points (e.g., V_0_1 means item 1 is measured at time 0). These load on 1 factor on 4 time points, thus Motivation0 means it's the factor at time 0. I am assuming items only correlate directly with itself on different time points. The model syntax is shown below:


Model2 <- ' 
# latent variables
Motivation0 =~ 1*V_0_1 + V_0_3 + V_0_4 + V_0_5 + V_0_6 
Motivation1 =~ 1*V_1_1 + V_1_3 + V_1_4 + V_1_5 + V_1_6
Motivation3 =~ 1*V_3_1 + V_3_3 + V_3_4 + V_3_5 + V_3_6 
Motivation4 =~ 1*V_4_1 + V_4_3 + V_4_4 + V_4_5 + V_4_6

# Item covariances

V_0_1 ~~ V_1_1 + V_3_1 + V_4_1
V_1_1 ~~ V_3_1 + V_4_1
V_3_1 ~~ V_4_1 

V_0_3 ~~ V_1_3 + V_3_3 +  V_4_3 
V_1_3 ~~ V_3_3 + V_4_3 
V_3_3 ~~ V_4_3 

V_0_4 ~~ V_1_4 + V_3_4 + V_4_4 
V_1_4 ~~ V_3_4 + V_4_4 
V_3_4 ~~ V_4_4 

V_0_5 ~~ V_1_5 + V_3_5 + V_4_5
V_1_5 ~~ V_3_5 + V_4_5
V_3_5 ~~ V_4_5

V_0_6 ~~ V_1_6 + V_3_6 + V_4_6
V_1_6 ~~ V_3_6 + V_4_6
V_3_6 ~~ V_4_6 


i =~ 1*Motivation0 + 1*Motivation1 + 1*Motivation3 + 1*Motivation4
s =~ 0*Motivation0 + 1*Motivation1 + 2*Motivation3 + 3*Motivation4

Motivation0 ~~ r*Motivation0
Motivation1 ~~ r*Motivation1
Motivation3 ~~ r*Motivation3
Motivation4 ~~ r*Motivation4

'
fit <- sem(model = Model, data = data, std.lv = TRUE, missing = 'FIML')

1) The above model / input gives me a working model. It took me a while to figure out, but what I have written in bold here is required for it. Could someone explain to me why I need to fix the variances of the Latent Variable / factor? If I don't, I get negative variances... probably because it's not identified - am estimating way too many variables then? Note: the above fit has 140df. 

2) When I don't use the marker variable method (i.e. fix one of the items for each time point / factor), I again get negative variances. That's probably related to 1, but I still don't get it why this happens. 

3) I am building this model after I already did some CFA model building. That is, not using the intercept (i) and slope (s) and using cfa(...), I got a decent model (i.e. decent GOF statistics). 

Thanks for your help.

Amonet

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Latent growth curve model: negative variances
parts: 1) The above model / input gives me a working model. It took me a while to figure out, but what I have written in bold here is required for it. Could someone explain to me why I need to fix the variances of the Latent Variable / factor? If I don't, I get negative variances...

So constraining residual variances to equality over time is not required, you are just trying to avoid negative variances.  Model misspecification can lead to negative variances (e.g., perhaps a linear slope is not appropriate), but so can sampling error (e.g., if you are estimating many parameters with not very many observations).

You can test whether the equality constraints are supported by the data by using a score test (only because those are the only 3 equality constraints in the model):

lavTestScore(fit, univariate = FALSE)

or with a likelihood ratio test, comparing models with and without the constraints.  If the constraints are not supported by the data, you should not include them simply to avoid negative variances.  You should investigate whether the negative variance estimate are consistent with model misspecification or with sampling error (or possibly both).
probably because it's not identified - am estimating way too many variables then? Note: the above fit has 140df.
This does not sound like an identification problem, nor does your syntax seem to imply an unidentified model.
3) I am building this model after I already did some CFA model building. That is, not using the intercept (i) and slope (s) and using cfa(...), I got a decent model (i.e. decent GOF statistics).

Decent?  If your problem is not with the measurement model, then there may be misspecification in the structural model.  Try comparing your linear growth model to a latent basis or quadratic growth model.
